entries.title: Background
entries.content: On 3 August 2024, student coordinators had announced a one-point demand — Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's resignation — and rejected her offer of talks at Ganabhaban. On the morning of 4 August, they launched a nationwide non-cooperation movement, urging people not to pay taxes or utility bills and not to report to work. Hasina repeated that the "doors of Ganabhaban are open" for negotiations; the student coordinators refused. The next day would be the deadliest single day of the uprising, with reporting citing figures ranging from early counts of 27 dead to approaching 90–100 by day's end, and a subsequent Wikipedia tally citing 97 dead including students.

entries.title: What Followed
entries.content: On 4 August 2024, violent clashes spread nationwide as protesters, police, and ruling-party activists clashed in Dhaka and other cities. A 16-year-old student, Golam Nafiz, was shot and fatally wounded by police at the Farmgate intersection around 4:30pm that afternoon; his death is recorded as a stated fact, without description of physical injuries. The government declared an indefinite nationwide curfew from 6pm. By evening, the student coordinators had announced a Long March to Dhaka for the next day. On the morning of 5 August, Army Chief General Waker-uz-Zaman and other senior military officials met with Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina at Ganabhaban and, per later reporting, urged her to resign. By afternoon, she had boarded a military helicopter with her sister and departed for India. Around 3pm that day, the Army Chief announced on television that Sheikh Hasina had resigned and that an interim government would be formed. Protesters stormed and occupied both Ganabhaban and the National Parliament House. The nationwide curfew was lifted and internet access was restored. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was proposed as chief adviser of an interim government, announced on 6 August and formed on 8 August 2024 — closing the acute-uprising period of July 2024.
